blocks.x: The End The End What's your name please?
My name is Paul Daniel Barnes, but my professional name is Paul Barnes.

And this is the first real, what's today's date? 16th of January, uh, Monday June. The end is 69. 69. Give me your full name. Barry Martin. And your what? And your name? Lloyd Elegant. Okay, boss. My name is Dick Allen, now let's try it again and see if the thing...
That's it. Okay, it's started. Well, uh, let me think. Paul, maybe the best thing is to get your date of birth first. What was your date of birth? When were you born?
I was born in New Orleans, Louisiana. On the 22nd of November, 1901. Uh-huh.
And, uh, when did you start playing? You know, what sort of, uh, how old were you?

Well, actually I've been playing since I was just a kid. I was six years old. And, uh, I didn't, I used to play a fight. We, kids, it was very popular in New Orleans. We, we would buy them for ten cents and, and we would play those fights. And a lot of the different musicians, Sidney, you take Sidney Bichet and George Lewis, my brother, and Mule Binger. We all start like that with those ten cents and fights. But, uh, I didn't begin to play professionally until 1919. That's, uh, I, I bought a saxophone on the third day of August. And on the third day of September I was, I was playing. Because I already had the foundation from the, playing those fights.
So you, you were playing saxophone before you played the clarinet, you mean?

Well, actually I played the clarinet first because my brother had a clarinet. When I was a kid I used to play his clarinet around. But when I got to play before the public, it was, it was the saxophone. Yeah.
What, uh, I guess the clarinets they had then were, uh, old-style. Uh, you use a BEM system clarinet now.
That's right. Uh, they had just a few fellas that would use the BEM system clarinet.
Uh-huh.
But they had old clarinets with fifteen keys. And some of them was fifteen keys.
Do you remember anybody who played the BEM system in those days?

When I first started playing clarinet, I, uh, bought a, uh, a BEM system clarinet. It was around nineteen, nineteen, twenty, I had just started playing already. But it looked like I couldn't get the hang of the clarinet, so I went back on the saxophone, and then just started playing the clarinet again until I got into the big band. But then I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't, I didn't have to take any solos or anything on the clarinet, all I did. When I had a solo, I'd take it on a soprano, because I was more familiar with the saxophone, at that time.
Did you have a teacher for all these instruments?

Um, practically self-learned. Because I had taken, what, three or four lessons from Miranda Theo. But he was always high all the time, so I didn't bother him. I just went right on. Studied and self-learned.
What instrument was Theo teaching you? I mean, clarinet or saxophone or, uh?
I learned clarinet from my brother, Neil. Oh, oh. But what I, what, the relative Theo should, taught me and gave me some of the ideas on saxophone.
When you started playing, I mean, did you, did your playing, did it favor anybody else, do you think, or?
I didn't understand.
When you started playing, did you, the way you played, did it sound like anybody else? Did you want to play like anybody else, or just your own style, or what?
I didn't want to play like Sidney Bessie, that was my inspiration. And I would try, as much as I could to play like him. But I just couldn't get the tone.
Yeah. What, uh, you ever played tenor saxophone? Tenor? Oh yeah, I played tenor.
I used to play tenor saxophone around New York.
Oh yeah?
Yeah. I played the baritone also. And the soprano.
What was the first band you played in, around here? You know, the first organized band.
The first, the first organized band that I played in, was my own band. And Lawrence, we got, we got, we made a band. And we called it the, the original Diamond Orchestra.
That's Lawrence Morera?

Yeah, Lawrence Morera and Joe Saia. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Who was Bush? Bush was a trumpet player. He was a fine trumpet player. He came up under Buddy P.T. Buddy P.T. was his instructor. He was the only one in the band who could read music. He helped me and Lawrence and the rest of the show to play the music. So I in turn helped Ray Allen. Yeah.
What was Bush's name? Bush Hall.
Thank you. Who taught you to read music Paul? Who taught you to read music? Me. Self study. Yeah. What you got a method? A method.
A method.
What kind of music did that band play? I mean you know the band with Ray Allen and Lawrence and what kind of numbers did they play?

Well we played traditional jazz music. But during that time we played the numbers like the Sheik of Arabi, and you know those numbers that was popular around the beginning of the 20s. And you played like dances?
That's right.
We played waltzes and see they used to play that back, they don't use it now, back in traditional times. The band didn't play a wall she wasn't considered. Yeah.

You were, in your style of music now you play a lot of harmony parts on the clarinet. Did you always play like that? You know what I mean? You play, your style of music you play a lot of harmony parts in the other couple of choruses, you played other harmonies to the lead. Did you always play that play?
Yes, but I played the lead also. But I do that when the trumpet is playing, and I play a second of the harmony. But I play both the lead and the big harmony. Yeah. I call it the second.
Yeah. What saxophone or clarinet players were there around in the early days, besides Sidney Bechet, which you liked to listen to? Who else was there, you know, that you liked to listen to?

Well there wasn't anyone outside of Sidney Bechet on the saxophone, but now the clarinet players around, after Sidney then left was Hall. I forget Hall's name, he played a thing with Louis Young, so he passed away. Edmund Hall? Edmund Hall, he was a very good clarinet player, I liked him very much. I always liked the Rinder Theo's clarinet player very much. But Sidney Bechet, he was chief.
What bands did you hear Sidney work with? I mean, who was he playing with at this time, Sidney Bechet?

At the time before Sidney left, he was playing with a band, they called himself, the Young Olympia band. And that was with Siren Moreira, and Buddy P.T. Sometimes Buddy would send Louis Armstrong into his place, and John Marrero. They had a wonderful band. Yeah.

Did the, I mean music, when you were coming out, was it the same sort of thing as now? I mean the trumpet would just play a couple of choruses in the lead, and then they'd take solos? No, no, they didn't do that.

See back in there, most of the trumpet would take down just for a few balls and wipe his lip, and he would play. But if he would get tired, the clarinet player would take a chorus and let him rest up his lip. But most of them, they were playing all the time. And the beat on the drum was different, back in the traditional music. They didn't hit that four beat, they didn't use that until the very last chorus when they were going out. What do you mean on the bass drum? As they played, they used, we used to call that a single beat. That's the same beat that you hear in a parade. That's the beat, that's traditional playing. And you just couldn't jump in anybody's band in those days and start beating four, four-four times. That came in with Dixaland music. Dixaland came from traditional New Orleans music.
Oh you mean they would play two beats in a measure on the bass drum?

Yeah, they'd make two beats. And they'd hit licks in there now, just like you hear the parade. That's why you hear the parade. But on the lads, whoever was leading the band, they'd stomp their feet and then they would go out. Then the bass would jump on four too, because the bass wasn't playing four all the way through, like in Dixaland. The bass would jump on four beats. And the drum, he would start all four, but he'd always hit a bass lick with the cymbal, like somebody clapping their hands. But not on the beat, after the beat. That was real traditional music. It had a tendency to move you. You even make a little baby feel like dancing. You know, hold on. But when Dixaland music came out, it came out putting four beats and playing plenty of bass music. You see? The fellas jumped all around with the instruments and showing themselves. But traditional jazz, they didn't do that. You know, you played, it's like I told you, you always played one beat until the last going out. Now the difference in the way of the playing, when you were playing Dixaland music, there was plenty of bass music and now and then you'd put a slow number in there or blues. But traditional jazz was more of a, it's called a fast track tempo. And now and then they would play a bass number or a slow number, a bogey bogey. It was most of them, it was moderate, most of them. Most of the tempo all the time was moderate. Or we used to call that a box track.
Of the drummers that are playing around New Orleans now, who would you say has the oldest style of all the drummers, you know?
Who is the one?
Who has the oldest style, do you think? If you could think of all the drummers, who's the one that has the oldest style?
Cali Piggott.
Cali Piggott? Yeah. He plays more like the, like you were saying?

Yeah, more like the original than any other. But he don't play long, because the fellas won't let him play it, they make him play the Dixaland style. So he's practically dying out now. Is Dave Bailey playing anymore?
Who?
Dave Bailey.

You know Dave Bailey. You live with Chris Cali. Oh. Is he still with him? Last time I talked to him, he was alive. I don't know. Yeah, yeah. He's just... Last time I talked to him, he was alive. Yeah, yeah. He's just... Last time I talked to him, he was alive. Yeah, yeah. He lives with John Henry McNeil uptown, but I don't know if you remember him or not. No, I do not. Yeah. Well, you played with him or not. Oh, yeah. I played with Chris. With Chris. Yeah, I played with everybody around here. Yeah, I played with everybody around here. I don't know if you remember him or not.
No, I do not.
Yeah. Well, you played with him, I know. Oh, yeah.
I played with Chris. With Chris. Yeah, I played with everybody around here. I played with him.
I noticed his drumming is quite... It's much freer. It doesn't pile up with playing two balls of this or four balls of that, you know, or 32 balls of this.
Well, probably he played more than traditional jazz. I don't remember playing with him. In fact, I don't remember him. But, Duck Arnie's brother.
Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah.
I see I'm not a guy.
Duck Arnie's brother. Half brother.
Yeah, yeah. Do you say you worked with Chris Kelly's band? I was not a regular member of his band, but I worked with his band. Do you remember when Emil worked in his band?
Yeah. He was with him a long time, huh?
Yeah. Yeah. That was his regular climbing player. Yeah. Sometime I would work with him on the, with the Alphurs Sax. Yeah.
Has Emil's playing ever changed, do you think? Emil's playing. Has it ever changed or has it always been that way? It's always been that way. That's all. Yeah.
And he never did play saxophone. Never did. Mm-hm. No. You ever worked with buddy Petit? I worked with them on the, with the alto sax.
Has Emile's playing ever changed? Has it ever changed or has it always been that way?
It's always been that way, just he was more familiar with his horn when he was young.
That's all. And he never did play saxophone?
Never did.
You ever worked with Buddy Petit?
Yeah, I worked with Buddy.
What was he like to work for?

Buddy is a wonderful trumpet player. But he played different from Kid Rene, in that he liked to run a lot of different, we used to call that changes, because of his horn. But if you would hear Louis Armstrong's old record, just like listening to Buddy Petit. But I don't mean Louis' late record, where he played all high in his pretty well. In the beginning, when he first started playing, he started to record in the ring of 20s, that you could get some of the records, you'd listen to Buddy Petit. Yeah.

You said that, remember that number we recorded the other day, Sand Dunes? You said that was one of Buddy's numbers? Is that where you first heard that number? By Buddy playing it? Did I? That number we recorded the other day, Sand Dunes. I understand. Is that where you first heard that number, by Buddy Petit playing it, or did you?
I first heard it with Kid Rene. But I did hear Buddy play it too. But Kid Rene, I used to play that number, with Kid Rene. That was one of his main numbers.
You were saying yesterday, not yesterday, when we came by here last, you were explaining to us that Kid Rene used to play it differently to Buddy. Do you remember? That who?
Kid Rene?
Kid Rene used to play that song, in a different way to Buddy. Oh yeah. And how was it different?
Well, it wasn't much difference, but it was, Rene would run a few eight notes, and you'd pick up on that number. And Buddy Petit would make it simple, you know.
That's all the difference.
You'd make a 20 minute simple pickup. You know, I tell you about that. Rene would run a scale up to the beginning of the melody. Yeah.
Do you remember when, were you in this town where Louis Armstrong went up north? Or were you up north then as well? I was in New Orleans.
You were here? I was here. Louis went to, I think Louis was when I first started playing. Because I started playing in 1919, professional. Yeah. I think Louis went up around 1920, I think.
1922, is it Dick?
I think so, but he went out on the boat of course before. Yeah.

Do you remember the records that he made with Joe Oliver? Do you remember, did any of them come down here? You know the records Louis made with Joe Oliver's band up there? Did you ever hear any of the records down here? That who made? Louis Armstrong, Louis Armstrong. Him and King Oliver, they made some records. Did you ever hear any of the records down here? Yeah. Did any of the- Yeah. I mean-
Did any of the- Yeah, I think- I believe Louis made- Snagit with King Oliver-
I think so, yeah.
And-
No.

No, I don't think he's on that- Mm-hm. Did you- No. Mm-hm. That- That King-Oliver's Big Band- Yeah. We're talking about the ones with Johnny Darius on clarinet and no sax- His first records- earliest records-
Was it with, you want to know if you did that with King Holland?
No, I said did you ever hear any of the records that they made down here, when you were down here?
Did any of the records get down here? Oh yeah, sure. All those records played, that survivor blues and all those records. Yeah. Heebie-jeebies. Oh yeah, yeah.
Were any of the bands around here influenced by Joe Oliver's band, by the records? Do you think? Yeah. You used to listen to them?
Anybody ask that question? Yeah, they were very much influenced by those bands.
When did they start using two trumpets?
When?
Yeah, I mean, you know on the Silestan records there's always two trumpet players.

Why did they have that? We started that in 1926 when we were recording, my number, Maya Josephine. That was 1926, they started using two trumpets. So we had Rick Carr, you know what I mean? Yeah, he was on that record, Maya Josephine, Rick Carr and Celestan. But after that the band started, they introduced the big bands. And that was around around 1926, 1927. After that's when I left Celestan and went with King Oliver and had me start using the real big bands.
Who else was in that saxophone section in the Celestan band? Do you remember who else was in the band?
When I was playing? Yeah. Yeah. A Sydney career and I can't think of Pierce's last name. Yeah, he's been with Eddie Pierce too. Not the trombone player, I must be. He's a saxophone player.
Is he any kind to Earl Pearson? Earl Pierce, yeah, that's what it is.

But it's Earl Pearson. Now we got it straight. What did he play? He played saxophone. What kind? He was playing third saxophone, I was playing first, and Sydney career was playing talent. So Earl Pearson played alto then?
That's right. Clarinets? Soprano, anything?
No, we didn't use it. We just had the saxophone. Just one? Yeah. I had the soprano though. I was the only one who used the soprano. Sydney career was using clarinet.
But what about on that first Celestan session though? How many, you know when you made Black Rag, Original Tuxedo Rag, and Careless Love?
Well, I don't think we had the big bands.
Who was in there? There were two saxes, huh? Two reeds, anyhow.
That was when B.B. Original was in the band. So fall back on it. What did you have? I think, and I was playing piano. Now I was playing sax. I don't know if sure enough it was Adolph Alexander.
Well, I've heard some people say Willard Tooney, and some people say, It could have been Willard Tooney, you know?

No, it wasn't a career. He hadn't come to the band then. It was either Willard Tooney, I think that's who it was. It was him or Adolph Alexander, probably it was Willard Tooney. So Willard, I got in the band just before Willard Tooney passed. Who used to write out arrangements for the saxophones?
Did you use any arrangements other than stock arrangements?
No, that's all we used stock arrangements. Two stocks? It was very popular stock arrangements.
Did Celestan direct the saxophone section or would he let you work out?
No, I had all that to do. In fact, I used to direct the whole band. Different things we would play mostly my ideas. I was a very important man to Father Celestan.
Would they, if you were playing a dance, would they like to play requests? Did they play requests? Yeah, we played requests.
We used to like to play requests.
Did you ever turn down any requests? No, never did.

We never turned down a request. We loved their requests. Suppose you didn't know the number, what would you do about it? Well, we'd just tell them we don't know that number. But anything else they'd like to hear, they would play for them.
How often did you get new stocks in? I mean, say two or three people came up and asked for a number, would you go out and buy the stock or not? Which way would you do it?
We wouldn't go out and buy the stock unless it was popular. Unless it was a real hit.
Yeah, that's right.
But someone asked us for a number that's popular, we would go ahead and buy it.
That band was reading all the time. Did all this play for music, the Salisdain band?

Most of the playing was reading at that time. But later on we started playing a lot of music just from memory. Salisdain, well a few numbers Salisdain would play, and I would just get behind him. And I thought so he would play without music. But when I first got a man, Salisdain would play without music unless he played Home Sweet Home or Eliza Jane or something like that. Whoa, Nellie.
What about my Josephine? Did you write an arrangement on that or did you play it by him? Or how did you work that out?

The way I worked that out, I just told him how I wanted to play. We didn't use any music. All the music we had was the fourth album for Salisdain. I wrote that music out for Salisdain and all the Salisdain. And all the rest of us followed his lead and I showed him how I wanted to play it.
And that tune wasn't published, I was never published that tune, was it? They never published it?
No, no I never published it. I got the copyright on it, got it right there, but I never did publish it.
You don't have any music to it in that way?
No, I don't have any music to it. But I'm thinking I'll have it published. I just don't have the copyrights for it, you know.
Do you remember what key it was written in?

G. Oh yeah. But if I would have it printed now, it would be in F. I would put it in F, that's low. Almost all the numbers that were written in G, bands up to there played in F. And that's the one tone lower, and make the band be heavier. Remember like St. Louis Blues? That was in G. Way down yonder in New Orleans, that was all that was in G. But the band dropped them down to F.
Did they used to play in G in those days? Yeah. I mean if the tune was published in that key, you used to play in that key.
They didn't change the key. They played, but when they get familiar they drop it down to F. It would save the trumpet player, each note would be on one tune lower.
It was a lot easier to play in F than G on a land instrument. That's right. I mean F is, flat keys are easier than sharp keys. And then it's F.
See F is one tone lower than G. Now each note that he makes is one tone lower. It's so much easier.

That reminds me, is there anybody around that really gets down and plays those pedal notes like they used to? I never have understood what happened to- On the trumpet? Yeah, like trumpet players. What happened to pedal notes playing?

Very few of them. That's what I was telling you just a while ago, but if you're listening to Louis Armstrong, and you were just like hearing Buddy P.T. You make those little notes. They don't seem to do that much anymore. Everybody wants to make high notes. In the modern style everybody wants to play flute parts. Trombone, trumpets, everything. Play out all of them. Play up like a flute and make a lot of notes. Who can make the most notes? There's a lot of different, she traditional, they're not interested in making a lot of notes. They want to make the feelings to make you feel. That's why I say this late rock and roll music that they play, and it's more like traditional jazz than any other music from that time. Even from, it's more even than the Dixaland and Bop music. All that late music that came out, all that fast work. But some of those records that you hear now, with the rock and roll, it's just like that traditional jazz. You hear how the bass player hitting each note. Bo-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba-bum-ba
Tuxedo band. South Stan?
Yeah, South Stan, tuxedo band.
What did you tell South Stan when you wanted to leave?
I just told him I was going to go, and he was glad for me. He hated to lose me, but he thought it was a good opportunity for me.
Did King Oliver write to you, or did he call you, or what?

King Oliver wrote to me. But he got to me through Manuel Perez. See, Manuel Perez at that time used to send all the best musicians up to the country, with King Oliver. Whenever they'd need something, Manuel Perez would be the man that would send the musicians up there. So he wrote to Manuel and Manuel got to me and then he wrote to me. Had John ever heard you play? He heard me. My recall, he never heard me play at first. I wasn't even playing when he left here. But after he heard that recalling on my Josephine, and the nice work that I did, he was very much anxious to get me up there with his band.
Where did you join him?

St. Louis, Missouri. It was Red Allen, Willie Foster, and me. We joined the King Oliver Band in St. Louis. Everybody left from St. Louis to New York. He played in the Savoy Ballroom. What kind of fellow was he, Josephine?
And what did he like to do? Strictly business. Everything on a business basis, huh?

That's right. But he'd find time to laugh and joke with the men all the time. Very advised fellow, you never had much to say in the band, you only had someone else to tell the fellows what to do. Really? Yeah, he'd never tell you anything.
Who would do the telling then, I mean, when you joined the band, who would really rock the band?
Well, Louis Russell, Louis Russell did all of that.
Was he doing a range here in the band? Was he doing a range here?

Yeah, he'd do some range, he was doing a range. And we had Kid O'Reilly on trombone, but Louis Russell did all of that. After that band broke up, we went on the road. We had trombone played, they did all the business. Pete, I can't think of his name unless I look up the name.
I think I have it outside in the car. Yeah. I didn't want to get it if you wanted to.
No, it wouldn't be necessary. But anyway, he was the one to tell the fellows all what to do.
Who used to pay off in the band? Did you all ever pay off the fellows? No. Just one second. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
The second track of Paul Vaughn, Reel 1, June 16, 1969. We're talking about paying off, huh, Baron? Oh, yeah. Yeah, I was asking you, who used to pay off the band to do it with Joe Oliver?

Joe Oliver never pays off himself. He always had someone who wanted to take that. Now, Clarence Black, when I first went out there, Clarence Black is the director. And he would do the paying off. He tend to have been.
